attribution: Traditionally attributed to Shankara; authorship debated by scholars, many of whom consider it a later Advaita work
period: Traditionally 8th century CE; scholars who doubt Shankara's authorship place it later, possibly well into the second millennium
summary: A long verse dialogue between a teacher and a disciple, laying out the Advaita path from qualifications of the seeker to liberation.
whyRead: The 'crest-jewel of discernment' is among the most popular introductions to Advaita, combining doctrine with devotional warmth and vivid images. It is a good bridge between beginner primers and the classical commentaries.
story: A disciple, tormented by the suffering of worldly existence, approaches a teacher and asks how to be freed. The teacher praises the question and unfolds the teaching over several hundred verses, ending with the disciple's expression of realisation and gratitude.
questions: How is the Self distinguished from the body and mind?
What is the liberated person like?

keyTeachings.title: The fourfold qualification
keyTeachings.text: The seeker needs discernment between the eternal and non-eternal, dispassion, six virtues beginning with calm and self-control, and a longing for liberation (sadhana chatushtaya).

keyTeachings.title: Self is not the sheaths
keyTeachings.text: The text works through the body, breath, mind, intellect and bliss sheaths, showing each to be non-Self.

keyTeachings.title: Discernment as the key
keyTeachings.text: Viveka, discrimination between Self and non-Self, is the jewel of the title; liberation follows from it, not from ritual or learning alone.

keyTeachings.title: The liberated while living
keyTeachings.text: Later verses describe the jivanmukta, one liberated while still embodied.
